query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a controlled, small amount (~2 at.%) of a lightweight element (e.g., Al) during synthesis of a refractory high-entropy alloy will induce the formation of finely dispersed nano-scale precipitates that enhance high-temperature creep resistance while minimally affecting the alloy density and preserving room-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., a lower-density variant based on Nb, Mo, Ta, W or similar) produced by standard arc-melting, exhibiting a mostly single-phase microstructure without Al addition.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled ~2 at.% aluminum addition at the alloy synthesis stage, followed by a post-solidification heat treatment designed to trigger nano-scale precipitate formation.
generation.conditions: High-temperature mechanical testing at approximately 1200°C under sustained load (creep or constant-load tensile conditions) and standard room-temperature tensile testing.
generation.structural_mediator: Nano-scale precipitates formed by the aluminum addition, dispersed uniformly within the alloy matrix.
generation.mechanism: The nano-precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion at elevated temperatures (precipitation strengthening), thereby increasing creep resistance, while the low density of Al ensures that the overall mass is not significantly increased and the room-temperature ductility is maintained.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline undoped alloy, the aluminum-doped alloy is expected to display a marked improvement in high-temperature mechanical capability (enhanced creep resistance) with similar tensile properties at room temperature and only a minimal increase in density.
generation.baseline: The same refractory high-entropy alloy synthesized without Al addition and processed under identical arc-melting and heat-treatment conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect may be limited to the specific processing conditions that ensure stable, nano-scale precipitate dispersion; if the Al content exceeds the optimal level or if heat treatment causes coarsening of precipitates, room-temperature ductility or density may be adversely affected.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal Al concentration and the magnitude of high-temperature strength improvement are not precisely known and may vary with the specific alloy system and processing details.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two batches of the refractory high-entropy alloy: one with ~2 at.% Al addition and the other without any Al addition. Both batches should undergo identical arc melting and post-solidification heat treatment protocols. Conduct microstructural characterization (TEM, XRD) to verify the presence and distribution of nano-scale precipitates. Then, perform high-temperature (≈1200°C) constant-load creep tests and room-temperature tensile tests on specimens from each batch.
measurements: Creep rate and rupture life at 1200°C under identical constant-load conditions
Tensile yield strength and ductility at room temperature
Microstructural metrics (precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the Al-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in high-temperature creep resistance compared to the undoped alloy, or if the addition of Al adversely affects the room-temperature mechanical properties (strength and ductility) or increases the density beyond acceptable limits.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . Abstract High entropy or compositionally complex alloys provide opportunities for optimization towards new high-temperature materials. Improvements in the equiatomic alloy Al 17 Co 17 Cr 17 Cu 17 Fe 17 Ni 17 (at.%) led to the base alloy for this work with the chemical composition Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (at.%). Characterization of the beneficial particle-strengthened microstructure by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and observation of good mechanical properties at elevated temperatures arose the need of accomplishing further optimization steps. For this purpose, the refractory metals hafnium and molybdenum were added in small amounts (0.5 and 1.0 at.% respectively) because of their well-known positive effects on mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys. By correlation of microstructural examinations using SEM with tensile tests in the temperature range of room temperature up to 900 °C, conclusions could be drawn for further optimization steps. Keywords: HEA, high entropy alloys, compositionally complex alloys, mechanical characterization

chosen.lever: controlled addition of a lightweight alloying element (e.g., optimized Al content)
chosen.technique: standard arc-melting synthesis combined with post-solidification heat treatments designed to precipitate nano-scale phases
chosen.conditions: High-temperature mechanical tests (≈1200°C under creep or constant-load conditions) combined with room-temperature tensile assessments to confirm preserved ductility; microstructural characterization (e.g. TEM, XRD) to verify precipitate distribution
chosen.why: This intervention directly fills the niche by using a composition change that introduces a lightweight element to trigger nano-precipitate formation. The precipitates are anticipated to retard dislocation motion at high temperatures, thus enhancing creep resistance, without significantly increasing the alloy’s density or degrading its room-temperature performance. This approach leverages well-established synthesis and characterization methods in refractory high-entropy alloys.
